newsitem.title: INDIA: Clouds hang over India's industrial output.
newsitem.headline: Clouds hang over India's industrial output.

text.p: Signs point to a dramatic slowdown in growth of India's industry but experts said on Wednesday they remain convinced production will begin accelerating later this year.

Last week the government reported that industrial output -- a key barometer for the overall economy -- inched up by only 2.4 percent in February over the same month in 1996. The growth rate in February 1996 was a blistering 13.3 percent.
Between April 1996 and February 1997 -- the first 11 months of the last fiscal year -- industrial production expanded by seven percent, down from 11.8 percent in the same period in 1995/96.
Tight credit, slack demand, heavy inventories and lack of power contributed to the growth slowdown, industry leaders said.
The government's most recent forecast in February projected an 8.7 percent expansion of industrial output in 1996/97.
But the independent Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) believes the growth rate was far less robust.
CMIE executive director Mahesh Vyas said his Bombay-based group expects the 1996/97 industrial growth rate to be between four and six percent.
"I am inclined to believe it will be at 4.5 percent," Vyas told Reuters.
An economist with a foreign securities firm was a bit more bullish on growth. "The general expectation is that industry will post growth of around seven percent in 1996/97," he said.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral on Monday lamented bottlenecks in the ailing infrastructure sector that he said have hampered expansion. The CMIE estimates power generation grew by only 3.1 percent in 1996/97 to 33,063 megawatts.

But analysts said they expect output to gather momentum in the third and fourth quarters of 1997/98 -- six months from September 1997 -- as the effects of increased bank credit, falling interest rates, lower corporate taxes and agricultural growth take hold.

"To stage a recovery, it is going to take some time. From September, October onwards, the pick-up will be faster," said V. Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce (Assocham).
Raghuraman predicted industry would grow by about eight percent in the 1997/98 fiscal year which began on April 1.
A.S. Kasliwal, president of Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), was less sanguine.
"Industry still has lot of inventory, and capacity utilisation has not yet picked up," he said, predicting industrial growth of 6.5 to seven percent in 1997/98.
The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) was more optimistic, projecting growth of 12 percent in 1997/98.
"The budget, along with increased credit availability, has improved the investment climate," CII spokesman Manashi Roy said.
"It will not be double-digit growth," Vyas said, adding: "We hope it will pick up after the monsoons, closer to September."
The government has forecast normal rains during the June-September monsoon season, which provides 80 percent of total average rainfall.

But this year's monsoon arrived 10 days late, and government meteorologists have said El Nino warm water currents have exhibited an "unfavourable trend" that should be monitored because of their likely adverse impact on monsoon rainfall.
